title: NVDA Stock Clocks Worst Week In 18 Years As SEC Reportedly Probes Its Accounting Practices - TradingView
content: Shares of Nvidia (NVDA) tumbled 14% on Friday, extending a steep multi-week slide following a report that the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission enforcement staff are examining potential accounting issues at the company. The agency is scrutinizing Nvidia’s accounting practices, Reuters reported, citing two people familiar with the matter. The Wall Street Journal had reported earlier in the week that the SEC was investigating the chipmaker but could not determine the probe’s focus. Reuters said it could not immediately establish when the inquiry began or which specific accounting matters are under review. An investigation does not prove wrongdoing and often end without enforcement action, the report noted. NVDA stock lost 23% this week, its worst since October 2008. The stock also clocked seven consecutive weeks of losses after Friday’s closing. The reported accounting focus adds to existing challenges for Nvidia as investors remain bothered by revelations involving former CEO Jensen Huang’s personal relationships, including one with Alice Huang, whom U.S. authorities suspect of being a Chinese spy—an allegation Beijing has denied. Alice Huang previously led Singapore-based Megaspeed, historically a large Nvidia customer. Jensen Huang acknowledged an extramarital affair last week without naming Alice Huang. The CEO’s statement was followed by more reports of romantic involvement with employees and Nvidia announced that it is probing the CEO and any potential compromise of company secrets or national security. Huang resigned as CEO of the chipmaker last week and the company said earlier this week that its board is not eyeing bringing him back. The company is now being led by former CFO Colette Kress, who has taken over as interim CEO while the company looks for someone to replace Huang. The Justice Department is separately reviewing Nvidia’s $12.9 billion deal to acquire open-source platform Hugging Face as part of a wider antitrust inquiry into the company’s acquisitions and practices. The department is also probing Megaspeed for potential violations of U.S. export controls involving advanced Nvidia AI chips, though the company itself has denied any wrongdoing. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around NVDA stock stayed within the 'extremely bullish' territory over the past 24 hours, while message volume stayed at 'extremely high' levels. He's referring to AI-related companies he publicly shorted over the past few years. In addition to the entire semiconductor industry, Burry called out GPU giant Nvidia and neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius. Although Burry claimed he "didn't say short" any of these companies, he maintains that he "provided the information one would need to sell." And Burry doesn't seem to see a bottom for the tech market anytime soon. In another X post, he compared today's market volatility to historic crashes in 1929 and 2000. Burry's primary reason for this correlation is "the lack of a proximate cause in earnings." On Substack, Burry expanded on this point, admitting that, although today's market leaders are "killing it with respect to earnings," that's no reason to expect higher prices. He cited articles from 1929 and 2000 to show how investors were in "complete shock that stocks were falling despite good news in earnings." The same phenomenon, Burry argued, is at play today with AI companies.​ To bolster his bearish thesis, Burry highlighted two other points. First, the peaks of the 1929 and 2000 rallies "predated real business deterioration by a year or so." Second, plenty of "bear market rallies" can follow a major collapse. According to his analysis, these false signs of hope had averaged 22% in bearish periods between 1929 - 1932 and 2000 - 2002.​ ​On X, Futurum Equities' Chief Market Strategist Shay Boloor pushed back against Burry's warnings, claiming Burry couldn't have predicted multiple black swan events that precipitated today's drawdown. Specifically, Boloor pointed to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's shocking resignation and Democrats winning traditionally red states like Texas. ​In response, Burry said, "If you think this is still all about an affair and some politics, you're not thinking hard enough."​ As the Jensen Huang scandal continues to unravel, Burry has been putting out more articles critical of Nvidia's business deals and their impact on the AI space. Another question Burry has with Nvidia is just how many of its chips made their way to the Asian market without government approval. In another X post, he commented on data suggesting some of the largest AI labs in China have been using banned Nvidia chips. As Burry said: "This is no surprise to analysts who years ago questioned SE Asia/Singapore's need for so many advanced $NVDA chips. The real reveal would be evidence that NVDA booked more revenue and profit from Asia than it had let on." Read More: Vanguard sees a slower decade for US stocks. For instance, at the time of writing, Nvidia's year-to-date performance is down about 27%, while riskier neoclouds like CoreWeave are in the red by roughly 43%. All of this selling pressure pushed the tech-heavy NASDAQ into slightly negative territory for 2026. At the time of writing, even diversified funds like the S&P 500 are now only up about 2% year-to-date. It can feel tempting during these times to join the crowd and panic-dump your portfolio. While everyone's situation is different, keep in mind that steep corrections in major indices are far from unusual. Data from Teachers Insurance and Annuity Association of America (TIAA) puts drawdowns into perspective. Declines of at least 5% in the S&P 500 happened in 94% of years post-1928. Even steeper dips of 10% or more happened in 63% of years throughout this period. Thankfully, rebounds are also common. For example, TIAA noted that although the S&P dropped 25% intra-year in 2022, it came roaring back in the subsequent three years with gains of 24%, 23%, and 16%, respectively. Of course, there are no guarantees on future prices, and people exposed to individual companies may have to make tougher decisions. Shares of Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) fell 14% on Friday afternoon, to less than $126, after Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating the chipmaker's accounting. The drop erased roughly $491 billion in market value in a single session, taking Nvidia from about $3.52 trillion to about $3.03 trillion. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Zoom out and the damage is even bigger. Nvidia closed at a record $239.24 on Oct. 6. At Friday's price, the stock is down about 48% from that high, and the company has lost about $2.7 trillion in value in just six weeks. Here's what we know, and what investors should make of it. The Wall Street Journal first reported on Tuesday that the SEC was investigating Nvidia but couldn't say what the probe was about. On Friday, Reuters, citing two people briefed on the matter, reported that the agency's enforcement staff are examining potential accounting issues at the company. Many questions remain unanswered. Reuters couldn't determine when the inquiry began or which accounting practices are under review. The SEC declined to comment, and Nvidia didn't immediately respond. Keep in mind that the SEC investigates plenty of companies that are never charged with anything. The stock was already having a bad day before the report: shares were down more than 6% earlier in the session amid a broad sell-off in AI stocks. The probe adds to a pile of problems. Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on Nov. 11 following revelations about his personal relationships, including with a woman U.S. authorities suspect of spying for China, which China denies. The Justice Department is also reviewing Nvidia's planned $12.9 billion purchase of Hugging Face, according to Reuters. Two areas could draw scrutiny. The first is how Nvidia reports where its sales come from. The company breaks out revenue by where customers are headquartered, rather than where they're billed. On that basis, about 63% of last quarter's revenue came from U.S.-based customers. The Financial Times has reported that Nvidia made the switch as sales billed to Singapore approached half of its total, a bad look with Southeast Asia having become a hub for chips smuggled into China. The second is how Nvidia helps its customers pay for its chips. On Tuesday's earnings call, interim CEO Colette Kress said Nvidia's guarantees totaled $118 billion at the end of the quarter, including $105 billion of credit support tied to a single data center campus. These guarantees are the kind of disclosure the SEC is watching closely at AI companies. When a chipmaker helps fund the projects that buy its chips, it's harder to tell how much demand would exist on its own None of this has shown up in the numbers yet. Nvidia's revenue jumped 103% to $115.8 billion last quarter, and the company expects about $130 billion this quarter. Management even raised its growth forecast for next fiscal year to about 75%. At about $126, the stock trades at roughly 12 times last quarter's adjusted earnings of $2.68 per share on an annualized basis, cheap for a company growing this fast. But cheap can get cheaper. Accounting questions hit at the heart of what investors pay for: trust in the numbers. Until Nvidia names a permanent CEO and the SEC's focus becomes clearer, the stock could stay volatile, even after a 48% drop. For long-term investors who already own Nvidia, there's no need to panic-sell on a report about an investigation. For anyone thinking of buying, it's smarter to wait for more clarity, or to build a position slowly, than to bet that the worst is over. There are plenty of other semiconductor stocks without a cloud of investigations hanging over them. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. If you'd invested $5,000 then, you'd be sitting on $1,897,590 today.* Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It's a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. The S&P 500 (^GSPC -3.70%) and the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -5.28%) are down 2.2% and 3.6%, respectively. Stocks stumbled around the world after the record IPO of the AI company Anthropic failed to restore investors' faith in AI -- an industry vital to the overall market, with 49% of the S&P 500 directly linked. AI stocks have had a tough go for some time now, with concerns over ballooning costs and limited value realized outside of specific applications -- namely, coding. Many investors were looking to the Anthropic IPO as a sort of "shot-in-the-arm" for AI stocks. content: NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) is trading at $141.64, down about -3.0%. The stock saw -3.30% fall yesterday and extended its losing streak to 6 sessions. The decline came after California’s attorney general issued a subpoena to the company and Anthropic’s debut failed to lift AI trade. Today, the market cap of NVDA is at $3.42 T. In its Q3 report, NVIDIA reported a year-over-year gain in revenue of about +103% with $115.8 B in that quarter. However, the analysts expectations were $109.1 B for the Q3 revenue. EPS also beat the analysts forecast of $2.48 and came in as $2.68 with +111% surge. As for profit, GAAP Net-Income came in at $65.3 B. The gross margin was also reported as 74.8%, which is up 1.4 points from previous year. Meanwhile, Data Center revenue rose +110% to $107.6 B, which is 93% of the total revenue. Given these numbers, it is clear that NVDA has a strong demand in market and is performing well across main parts of business. Another positive surprise was the Q4 outlook. The company expects the Q4 revenue around $130 B. Meanwhile, the Wall Street analysts anticipation sits at $125.1 B. However, the guidance does not include any Data Center compute revenue from China. Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on 12th Nov and CFO Colette Kress is now the interim CEO. The board said it does not intend to reinstate Huang, and it is searching for a permanent CEO. On the other hand, California’s attorney general subpoenaed the company over whether its chips reached China, and the SEC is reportedly investigating, which added some selling pressure on stock. Another concern is that customers owed NVIDIA $81 B at the end of the quarter, which is about 64 days of sales. Any payment delay could hit price movement quickly. On valuation side, NVDA trades at a trailing P/E of 16 and a forward P/E at 10. The average Wall Street analysts consensus rating is Buy for the stock with 3 Strong Buy, 43 Buy, and 15 Hold ratings. The average price target by them is $224.50. Currently, the price target by Freedom Broker was lowered to $230 from $305. Whereas, William Blair downgraded the stock to Market Perform and RBC maintained its Outperform rating with a price target of $230. NVDA is trading below its 20-D moving average of $189 and its 200-D average of $204. The stock briefly slipped below $140 to about $138.90 after the open before bouncing, so the initial support remains at $140 level with the next support S2 at $135 level. On the upside, initial resistance lies at $145.98, with the longer term resistance point at $158.13. Any close above $145.98 could keep NVDA moving toward $150.96. On the other hand, any close below $140 could drag the price towards $135. For now, investors are focusing on the CEO search and the regulatory probes. NVIDIA stock is falling amid CEO uncertainty, regulatory probes by California’s attorney general and the SEC, and continued weakness in the broader AI trade. Wall Street analysts have an average price target of $224.50, with a consensus Buy rating. However, some analysts have recently lowered their targets or downgraded the stock. NVIDIA delivered strong Q3 results and issued better-than-expected Q4 revenue guidance. However, CEO uncertainty, regulatory investigations, and concerns about customer payments are weighing on investor sentiment. The $140 support level is important to watch, while $145.98 is the first resistance. A break below $140 could expose NVDA to further downside toward $135.

title: Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) Posts Record $115.84B Quarter And Raises Annual Forecast Even As Leadership Crisis Deepens - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By Ewan Scott | Nov 20, 2026 | Featured, News & Analysis A chipmaker whose stock has shed nearly a quarter of its value this month just delivered one of the most impressive quarterly performances in semiconductor history. Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) reported third-quarter revenue of $115.84 billion on Tuesday, blowing past analyst estimates of $109.10 billion and more than doubling the $57 billion recorded in the same period a year ago. Adjusted earnings per share came in at $2.68, comfortably ahead of the $2.48 consensus figure compiled by LSEG, reinforcing the view that the underlying business remains operationally intact. The company’s data center division, its most critical revenue engine, generated $107.6 billion for the quarter, exceeding a Street Account estimate of $101.87 billion and more than doubling on an annual basis. Perhaps more striking than the results themselves was the guidance: Nvidia said revenue next quarter will reach approximately $130 billion, topping the $125.1 billion average analyst estimate, and raised its full fiscal year 2028 growth forecast to 75% from a previous target of 70%. The strong numbers arrive at a particularly fraught moment, as Nvidia navigates the abrupt resignation of co-founder Jensen Huang following the disclosure of a personal relationship with Alice Huang, a businesswoman alleged by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese spy. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, elevated to interim CEO last week after 13 years in the CFO role, led the earnings call and used it to project stability, declaring “It’s business as usual. We’ve engaged with our customers, we’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners. They’re all 100% behind us.” The China dimension remains the most tangible financial risk, with the Commerce Department moving to close a loophole that had allowed Chinese companies to rent Nvidia computing power located in other countries, and the company stating it is “not assuming any Data Center compute revenue from China in our outlook.” Nvidia’s board chair Harvey Jones confirmed on the call that Huang resigned after conduct “inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards and cultural norms,” and stated flatly that the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” even as Huang issued a public statement signaling openness to returning. Executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles has been retained to lead the permanent CEO search, with Nvidia board veteran Ian Buck, who helped create the CUDA software platform underpinning the company’s AI dominance, joining the earnings call for the analyst Q&A and viewed by some as a candidate. The leadership uncertainty has rattled investors and analysts alike, with more than 20 analysts tracked by FactSet cutting their price targets over the past nine days, including Mizuho, which lowered its target to $220 from $250 and cited what it called a “6-7 month management overhang.” Despite those concerns, the after-hours market reaction was broadly positive, with Nvidia shares climbing nearly 4% following the results, while neocloud operators CoreWeave, Nebius, and Iren each surged between 8% and 10% on confidence in the AI infrastructure buildout. title: Does Huang’s Exit Sink Nvidia Stock? History Is Split - Trefis
content: Today’s big story: Will 2027 Be A 2022 Repeat For Stocks? Nvidia’s board said on Tuesday’s earnings call that it does not intend to bring back Jensen Huang as CEO. Huang, the company’s co-founder, resigned with immediate effect on Nov 12. Most readers want to know who can run Nvidia without him. This article asks a different question. What happened to stocks when a founder left a market leader? The record gives no single answer. Our price data covers three founder-CEO exits at market leaders. A year later, Microsoft was down 48.0%. Apple was up 76.1%. Amazon was down 10.5%. Only Apple beat SPY, a fund that tracks the S&P 500, over one year and over three years. Here is how Nvidia has traded since the news. Nvidia fell 16.0% from the Nov 11 close to the Nov 19 close. The Nov 11 close was the last one before Huang resigned. Over the same days, Broadcom rose 0.4%. SPY fell 5.8%. On Nov 12, the day of the announcement, Nvidia fell 4.3%. Advanced Micro Devices rose 5.9% that day. Broadcom rose 5.5%. On day one, money left Nvidia while two other big chip makers rose. The board’s statement came on the evening of Tuesday, Nov 17. The results release went out at 4:20 pm, after the close. From the Nov 17 close to the Nov 19 close, Nvidia fell another 6.1%. Broadcom rose 1.5%. AMD fell 2.8%, and SPY fell 2.3%. Nvidia is down 16.0% since the last close before Huang resigned, and 6.1% since the board said he would not return. If Nvidia is a big part of your savings, a drop like that is hard to sit through without wanting to sell. The Trefis Income Solution fell less than the S&P 500 in each of the 9 big sell-offs since 2018, and it pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500’s. See how it held up. One way to check is operating margin. That is the share of each dollar of sales left after the costs of running the business. The table below shows each founder exit, the stock’s return against SPY, and the margin before and after. Source: Intrinio split-adjusted closing prices and Morningstar income statements. Returns are price only. They run from the last close before the news to the close 252 trading sessions (one year) and 756 sessions (three years) later. SPY is measured over the same sessions. Margins compare the last full fiscal year before the exit with the third full fiscal year after it. Microsoft’s margin fell from 50.9% to 41.1%. Its stock lost 51.4% over three years. Apple’s margin went from 28.2% to 28.7%. Its stock rose 87.2% over three years. Amazon breaks the pattern. Its margin rose from 5.9% to 10.8%. Yet its stock trailed SPY over one year and over three years. Three cases are too few to make a rule. We read them as examples, not odds. Nvidia’s case also differs from all three. Bill Gates handed the job to Steve Ballmer and stayed on as chairman. Steve Jobs became Apple’s chairman when he gave up the CEO job. Jeff Bezos said ahead of time that he would step down, and he stayed on as executive chair. Huang left with immediate effect and also left the board. The chief financial officer agreed to serve as interim CEO. Nvidia’s operating margin was 66.9% in the quarter to Oct 25, 2026. That was the last full quarter before Huang left. Revenue was $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier. The company’s guidance for its fourth quarter implies a GAAP operating margin of about 63.0%. That would be lower than the third quarter. In their latest reported quarters, AMD’s margin was 21.2% and Broadcom’s was 54.3%. We think the margin is the better test of Nvidia after Huang, though it is not a sure one. At Microsoft, the founder’s exit came with a falling margin. At Apple, the margin held. At Amazon, the margin rose, but the stock still trailed SPY. For the earnings case, see Why Huang’s Exit May Not Sink Nvidia Stock. Nvidia was already 27.4% below its Oct 6 record close before Huang resigned. At Thursday’s close, it was 39.0% below that record. Much of the fall came before the CEO news. The wider market also fell. SPY fell 2.0% on Thursday, Nov 19. AMD fell 11.5% from the Nov 11 close to the Nov 19 close. No company statement or filing says how much of Nvidia’s fall is about Huang. We cannot split it from the wider market’s fall. Nvidia has been this far below a high before. After first closing a third below its Nov 2021 high, it fell another 49.7% to a low in Oct 2022. It closed back at its Nov 2021 high on May 25, 2023. That was a different time, and past falls do not set the path of this one. This question is part of our coverage of the AI story. Our read: a founder leaving has not decided where a market leader’s stock went. We would watch whether Nvidia’s margin holds up. Until it settles, owners may face more drops like this week’s. Those drops are easier to sit through when the rest of your money falls less than the market does. Holding on is easier when your portfolio falls less than the market. MSCI's broadest Asia-Pacific index excluding Japan plunged approximately 8.5% for the week, while Japan's Nikkei 225 dropped 5.1% on Friday. South Korean memory chip manufacturers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix also fell roughly 6%-7% as investors reduced exposure to AI infrastructure suppliers. Japan's Nikkei finished at approximately 56,437 points, while the KOSPI closed near 4,870. Taiwan's benchmark recorded a weekly decline of approximately 17.5%, its steepest since 1991. According to Nvidia's official earnings release, third-quarter revenue reached $115.8 billion, increasing 103% year over year. title: Prediction: Nvidia Will Hit a New All-Time High in 2027 (Hint: Watch This Metric) - The Motley Fool
content: Nvidia has lost nearly 37% of its market value in recent weeks, but an epic recovery could be in store next year. It's been a turbulent November for Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%) as the company deals with the unexpected resignation of founder and longtime CEO Jensen Huang. Uncertainty surrounding the company's leadership transition, investigations involving ties to China, and questions about its artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure partnerships are weighing heavily on investor sentiment. Nevertheless, Nvidia's latest financial results suggest the company's business is expanding at a record pace. During its fiscal third quarter (ended Oct. 25), Nvidia generated $115.8 billion in revenue, representing 103% year-over-year growth. Meanwhile, adjusted earnings per share (EPS) climbed 111% to $2.68. Despite this impressive performance, Nvidia stock is trading roughly 37% below its all-time high. With that said, one financial metric could ultimately drive the stock to new highs: earnings per share (EPS). Nvidia has two opportunities to expand EPS over the coming year, combining organic profit growth with an enormous share repurchase program. Nvidia's first opportunity to increase EPS comes directly from its underlying business. The company is a key beneficiary of AI-driven demand from hyperscalers expanding their data center build-outs. Nvidia's data center division generated $107.6 billion in revenue during the third quarter, increasing 110% year over year. What's particularly impressive is Nvidia's ability to convert its top-line growth into substantial profits. During the third quarter, the company reported a gross margin of 74.8%. This reflects the pricing power associated with Nvidia's GPUs, networking products, and CUDA software ecosystem. These economics allow Nvidia to generate enormous profits alongside an accelerating revenue base. Although management expects gross margin to moderate to between 71% and 72% in the fourth quarter, it anticipates a recovery to between 72% and 73% in fiscal 2028. More importantly, interim CEO Colette Kress raised the company's fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook to approximately 75% year over year, up from its previous projection of 70%. Even if gross margin remains below its peak, Nvidia can still produce higher earnings through increased sales volumes and operating leverage. In other words, as revenue grows, certain operating expenses may increase at a slower rate relative to sales. This would allow additional revenue to contribute disproportionately to operating profits. The idea here is that Nvidia doesn't necessarily need to maintain record gross margins to achieve record earnings. Nvidia's second earnings catalyst is its share repurchase authorization. In September, Nvidia's board of directors approved a $150 billion increase to its existing repurchase program. As of the end of the fiscal third quarter, Nvidia had $227.3 billion remaining under its authorization. Management affirmed its intention to execute the remaining portion of the repurchase authorization by the end of fiscal 2028. This makes stock buybacks an important, albeit underrated, component of Nvidia's capital allocation strategy. The significance of Nvidia's share repurchases becomes clearer once you understand how EPS is calculated. Earnings per share equals a company's net income divided by its shares outstanding. When Nvidia repurchases and retires shares, the company effectively reduces the denominator in that equation. This means EPS can increase even if net income remains unchanged. For example, suppose a company generates $100 billion in annual net income across 25 billion shares. That would translate into EPS of $4.00. If the same company reduced its share count by 5%, while net income remained unchanged, EPS would increase to $4.21 without any additional revenue or profit growth. Stock prices are influenced by two interconnected variables: earnings per share and the valuation multiple investors are willing to pay for those earnings. A company's share price can rise even when its price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio remains unchanged, provided EPS increases. This unique relationship makes the mechanics around Nvidia's potential earnings expansion particularly interesting. Nvidia's combination of projected revenue growth, compounding profitability, and aggressive share repurchases creates a compelling outlook around next year's EPS. These catalysts provide the foundation for a bounceback in Nvidia stock even without assuming a dramatic increase in the company's valuation multiple. I think Nvidia stock could soar next year, driven by accelerating EPS growth rather than speculative enthusiasm. Against this backdrop, investors should monitor Nvidia's net income growth and changes in shares outstanding over the coming quarters. Taken together, these metrics could reveal whether Nvidia's financial performance is strong enough to overcome its recent challenges and propel the stock to new highs. After being a darling of the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution for nearly four years, Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) has become one of Wall Street's most controversial stocks following the unexpected resignation of founder and longtime CEO Jensen Huang. The company is facing mounting uncertainty around its leadership transition as investigations involving potential ties to Chinese intelligence and questions about its extensive AI infrastructure partnerships unfold. These developments have shaken investor confidence, sending Nvidia shares plunging despite the company's strong financial performance. On Nov. 17, Nvidia reported earnings for its fiscal third quarter. Total revenue grew 103% year over year to $115.8 billion, while adjusted earnings per share (EPS) surged 111% to $2.68. Management also forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion, implying 91% annual growth. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Legendary investor Warren Buffett's investment philosophy offers a compelling framework for evaluating Nvidia amid all of this uncertainty. Throughout his career, Buffett consistently emphasized durable competitive advantages, strong business economics, and the purchase of high-quality companies at reasonable valuations. These principles suggest Nvidia could remain an attractive long-term investment despite its current challenges. One of Buffett's most important investment principles is identifying companies with economic moats. These competitive advantages protect a business from rivals, allowing it to maintain market share and generate attractive returns over a long-term time horizon. Nvidia has several characteristics that make its competitive position difficult to replicate at scale. Perhaps its greatest advantage is the CUDA software ecosystem, which allows developers to optimize applications for Nvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs). CUDA has become deeply embedded in AI research and hyperscale computing infrastructure. This creates switching costs because customers considering a move to competing platforms need to modify applications, retrain developers, and validate the costs associated with new computing environments. Nvidia benefits from its extensive relationships with cloud providers such as Microsoft, Amazon, and Alphabet, as well as hardware manufacturers like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, Micron Technology, and Marvell Technology. This integrated approach stitches together Nvidia's GPUs, networking equipment, software, and accelerated computing systems. This end-to-end stack makes it difficult for competitors to replicate the platform as a whole. Although Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom's custom AI accelerators pose competitive headwinds, Nvidia's full-spectrum ecosystem provides protection beyond the performance of any individual chip. Importantly, these advantages are not solely dependent on Huang's personal relationships. They reflect decades of engineering investments, software development, and customer adoption that will remain in place following his departure. Buffett frequently emphasizes pricing power as a defining characteristic of outstanding businesses. Companies capable of raising prices without sacrificing customer demand usually maintain competitive advantages. Nvidia's financial performance suggests its products command extraordinary economic value even as investment in data center build-outs accelerate. During the third quarter, Nvidia generated a 74.8% gross margin. This means roughly three-quarters of its revenue remained after accounting for the direct costs of producing its products and services. That is an exceptional margin profile for a company rapidly expanding production of next-generation chip architectures. Nvidia's pricing power stems from the economic benefits its products provide to customers. Compute efficiency, energy consumption, and deployment speed have meaningful financial consequences for hyperscalers developing AI models and applications. Therefore, customers are willing to pay a premium for Nvidia's technology, as its performance and accompanying software can reduce overall operating costs. Perhaps Buffett's most relevant investment principle involves the relationship between business quality and purchase price. In his 1989 Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letter, Buffett famously wrote, "It's far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price." That philosophy is particularly relevant to Nvidia today. The company's record financial performance contrasts with its recent stock price decline. The question for investors is whether Nvidia's lower valuation now offers an opportunity to buy an exceptional business at a reasonable price. At roughly $149 per share, Nvidia trades at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 16 and a forward P/E ratio of 10. Those valuations are unusually modest for a business generating triple-digit revenue and profit growth. If Nvidia sustains even a portion of its current growth trajectory, today's valuation will eventually look attractive. Ultimately, Nvidia appears to satisfy several important criteria of Buffett's investment philosophy. While the company's future without Huang remains uncertain, its technological advantages and financial performance provide reasons for optimism. For investors willing to tolerate short-term volatility and maintain a long-term investment horizon, the recent sell-off represents an opportunity to buy the dip in Nvidia stock. On Oct. 6, Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) peaked at an intraday high of $243.37 per share, reaching a valuation of $5.78 trillion. The face of the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out holds a virtual monopoly in enterprise data centers with its several generations of graphics processing units (GPUs). But it's been a bumpy ride over the last six weeks. Between its Oct. 6 intraday peak and the Nov. 17 close, Nvidia lost $2.03 trillion in valuation. In just six weeks, Nvidia lost more in market value than all but five S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) companies... one of which is itself. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » While Nvidia's historically inexpensive valuation and its jaw-dropping Data Center segment growth suggest its stock is a bargain, it's also possible that its recent downtrend is just beginning. Let's not beat around the bush: the resignation of now-former CEO Jensen Huang following an admission of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy and allegations of extramarital relations with up to two employees has left Nvidia without an identity. Although Nvidia has an extensive order backlog, superior GPUs, and its pricing power continues to be aided by GPU supply shortages, the company's innovation schedule (bringing an advanced AI chip to market annually) and its circular financing deals are very much in question. Furthermore, Huang's actions and departure may have breached the trust of clients, consumers, and/or investors. Earlier this week, the Securities and Exchange Commission opened an investigation over whether the company misled investors in its disclosures. Without trust, Nvidia becomes practically uninvestable. Although long-term trends strongly suggest that AI will be a game changer and that the benchmark S&P 500 will head higher, historical precedent isn't Nvidia's friend over the short run. Every next-big-thing technology since (and including) the advent and proliferation of the internet in the mid-1990s has navigated an early-innings bubble. These bubbles form because investors consistently overestimate the pace of adoption and optimization of hyped innovations. The good news for AI is that there isn't an adoption issue. Nvidia's quarterly results make it clear that businesses are freely spending to build out their data centers. But it's an entirely different story when it comes to optimizing this technology. It took until well after the dot-com bubble burst before businesses figured out how to optimize internet-driven solutions to maximize sales and profits. As with the internet, AI will take time to mature, leaving Nvidia and its peers exposed to a possible bubble-bursting event. Lastly, Nvidia's fiscal fourth-quarter gross margin is forecast to dip to 71%-72% from a reported 74.8% (based on generally accepted accounting principles, or GAAP) in the fiscal third quarter. Although Nvidia's GAAP gross margin has pretty consistently hovered in the low-to-mid 70% range over the trailing three years, the company's fiscal fourth-quarter forecast must have some investors wondering if this is as good as it gets. NVDA Gross Profit Margin (Quarterly) data by YCharts. This two- to three-percentage-point dip in GAAP gross margin reflects higher memory prices and the near-term ramp-up associated with Vera Rubin shipments. But if GPU supply picks up from its competition, as is expected, Nvidia's pricing power and GAAP gross margin would be expected to wane over time. In other words, Nvidia may not be the slam-dunk bargain it appears to be. title: Is Nvidia’s $81 Billion Receivables Pile A Risk? - Trefis
content: Today’s big story: Will 2027 Be A 2022 Repeat For Stocks? Most talk about Nvidia stock centers on two events. Its CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned after the board cited personal behavior that broke the company’s code of conduct. The board said it does not intend to reinstate him. Nvidia also stopped shipping its licensed Hopper chips to China, a line worth $2.4 billion last quarter. This article looks at a different number. It is the money customers owe Nvidia, called receivables. Those receivables reached $81.0 billion on Oct 25, 2026. That equals about 64 days of sales. Our quarterly receivables data for Nvidia start in 2001. From April 2001 to July 2026, the average was 44.6 days. It rose every time. We flagged each quarter when receivable days ran at least 10 days above their average of the previous two years. Nvidia was higher 12 months later after all 11 completed flagged quarters. The median gain, the middle result, was 77.9%. The ride was often rough. After the July 2008 flag, Nvidia dropped another 48.7% before it turned up. A year after the start it was 31.4% higher. After the October 2018 flag, it slid another 25.3% first. Nvidia dropped another 48.7% after the 2008 flag before any gain showed up. If much of your savings rides on Nvidia, that is a long, scary slide to sit through. The Trefis Income Solution fell less than the S&P 500 in each of the 9 big sell-offs since 2018, and it pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500’s. See how it held up. Nvidia has risen after most quarters, so the fair test compares the flags with all quarters. Measured the same way, the stock was higher a year later after 73 of 97 quarters. The median gain for all quarters was 36.1%. The flagged quarters beat that on both counts. The table below sets the flagged quarters against all quarters, after six months and after a year. Source: Trefis company data from Morningstar (receivables and revenue) and Intrinio closing prices adjusted for splits and dividends. A quarter is flagged when receivable days are at least 10 days above the average of the previous eight quarters. Each return starts at the first close at least 35 days after the quarter ended, after Nvidia had reported. Back-to-back flagged quarters overlap, so we also counted them as single episodes. There were 7 completed episodes, and Nvidia was higher a year later in all 7. A looser test points the same way. It flags quarters one standard deviation above the average of all earlier quarters. A standard deviation is a common measure of how far a figure usually strays from its average. That test gives 22 of 24 cases higher a year later. Nvidia closed at $145.98 on Thursday, Nov 19. That was down 3.3% for the day. The stock is 39.0% below its Oct 6 close of $239.24. At about 64 days, October 2026 sat 12.6 days above the prior eight-quarter average of 51.1 days. July 2026 was 10.6 days above its own average. So this is the second flagged quarter in a row. The receivables balance rose by $18.0 billion in the October quarter alone. This time may not match the past. Past flags mostly came when sales were weak. Of the 11 completed flagged quarters, 6 came with revenue shrinking from the prior quarter and 3 with growth under 2%. This time revenue grew 20.4% from the July quarter to the October quarter. So customers owe more while buying more, which is a different setup from the past cases. This episode has also started badly. Our count for the July 2026 flag starts at $220.53, the Aug 31 close. That was the first close at least 35 days after the quarter ended. Nvidia is down 33.8% since then. About nine months of that 12-month window are left. The past record is small and its windows overlap. We read it as a record, not a forecast. The money to pay for chips also has to come from somewhere. Operating cash flow is the cash a business brings in from its daily work. Capital expenditure is money spent on buildings and equipment. Here is what four large tech companies brought in and spent in the September 2026 quarter. Three of them spent more than they brought in. Together they spent $26.4 billion more than they took in from operations. This question sits inside our AI storyline. We think the clearest sign would be customers paying down what they owe. In the October quarter, Nvidia’s cash flow statement shows that higher receivables used $18.1 billion of its cash. A year earlier the figure was $5.6 billion. If receivable days fall back toward the 44.6-day long-run average, the worry would ease. If they keep rising, the worry would grow. For the full story of the jump itself, see Why Do Nvidia’s Customers Owe It $81 Billion? Our read: a jump in what customers owe has not been a warning sign in Nvidia’s past. It has said little about how deep the fall could get before the gain came. The past gains went only to holders who sat through drops of up to 48.7%. Holding on is easier when your portfolio falls less than the market. New debt is borrowed debt, leases excluded, Sep 2025 to Sep 2026 (Oracle to Aug). Anthropic: commitments “expected to be incurred before December 31, 2030”, from its filing. Nvidia: Oct 6 to Nov 19 close, dividend-adjusted. Customers want more AI computing than exists. The builders can’t wait, because of what happened in cloud, the last big race. There, the companies that built first are the three that now earn about $150 billion a year of operating profit. Operating profit is profit from the business before interest and taxes. So why does anyone worry? Demand that can’t be stopped can still arrive later than the bills. That happened in 2000. That year Verizon spent $1.11 on its network for every dollar of cash its business brought in. Two years later it cut that spending 31%. The companies selling it the gear fell 89% to 99%. When the builders last paused, in 2023, Meta’s stock soared. Meta cut its spending 13%. Its free cash more than doubled, and its stock rose 194% that year. The companies that sold them equipment took a generation or more to recover. The phone companies all cut their spending in 2002. By then, the equipment makers’ stocks had fallen 89% to 99%. The big buyers cut at the same time. Verizon cut its spending 31% in 2002. SBC, today’s AT&T, cut 39%. In our view, no one wanted to be the last one still building when there was already too much. The buyers’ stocks fell hard. Verizon fell 54% from its high. But their businesses kept running. The sellers, such as Cisco, Juniper and Corning, were hit harder. title: Is Nvidia Stock a Once-in-a-Decade Buying Opportunity After Its Latest Earnings? - The Motley Fool
content: There is a light at the end of the tunnel for Nvidia. By Prosper Junior Bakiny – Nov 19, 2026 at 4:15PM EST The past week has been hard on Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%). The semiconductor leader had to separate from its co-founder and now-former CEO, Jensen Huang, after he was embroiled in a scandal involving alleged extramarital affairs, including with a woman believed to be a Chinese intelligence asset. Colette Kress, who remains CFO, has stepped up as interim CEO, leading the company through its first quarterly update since Huang's departure. And what an update it was. Nvidia once again crushed expectations, but that wasn't enough to jolt the stock, which remains down significantly since it reached a new all-time high in early October. Is Nvidia a generational buying opportunity at current levels? Death, taxes, and Nvidia's financial results coming in above analysts' projections seem to be the only certain things these days. In the third quarter of its fiscal year 2027, which ended on Oct. 25, the company's revenue came in at $115.8 billion, up 103% compared to the year-ago period. Data center revenue grew 110% year over year to $107.6 billion. Nvidia's non-GAAP gross margin was 74.9%, compared to the 73.5% reported in the prior-year quarter. The semiconductor specialist's non-GAAP operating income was $77.9 billion, rising 116% year over year, while its non-GAAP earnings per share were $2.68, up 111% year over year. The fact that profits are growing faster than revenue is a strong sign for Nvidia, given the industry's increasing competitiveness. While some investors worry that competition from custom AI chips will erode the company's pricing power in the GPU (graphics processing unit) market, as hyperscalers and other corporations increasingly opt for these custom chips, it seems, at least, that this hasn't happened yet. Improving margins are a sign that Nvidia maintains strong pricing power. Meanwhile, Nvidia's free cash flow for the period was $43.8 billion, rising 98% year over year. The company also posted excellent guidance. Nvidia expects $130 billion in revenue (at the midpoint) for its fourth quarter. That would represent a 91% year-over-year increase. Somebody is going to make a fortune on Anthropic’s IPO. It probably won’t be regular investors waiting for the day it goes public. Unless investors know where to look. Because two companies anyone can buy today already own pieces of Anthropic. And one of them owns a piece of OpenAI, too. Of course, Nvidia's financial results and guidance were only part of the story. The market wants to know how the company's efforts to replace Huang are going. Nvidia said it isn't interested in bringing back Huang, despite many people, both inside and outside the company, calling for his reinstatement. And it is actively looking for a replacement, although nobody knows when Nvidia will find someone to step into the CEO role permanently. In my opinion, that's both good and bad. It's bad because the longer this search drags on, the more uncertainty it could add to the company's prospects. But it's good because replacing a CEO as effective as Huang isn't an easy task, and the company's board is rightfully taking the time it needs to do so, or so it seems. In the meantime, several factors highlight just how massive an opportunity Nvidia could still tap into, even as it faces a more stringent regulatory environment. During the recent U.S. midterm elections, voters elected many lawmakers and politicians across various states who had promised to be stricter on the AI industry. This may result in delayed permits and slower data center build-outs. However, Nvidia expects a great year ahead. The company raised its guidance for the fiscal year 2028, which covers most of the calendar year 2027. The company now expects revenue to grow 75% in fiscal year 2028, up from its previous projection of 70% -- and that's after also raising its guidance for its current fiscal year. If we assume Nvidia's fourth-quarter revenue lands at the midpoint, it could generate $423.7 billion this fiscal year and $741.4 billion next year, based on its projected 75% growth rate. So, given its current market cap of $3.8 trillion, Nvidia is trading at 5.1x estimated fiscal year 2028 revenue -- that's more than fair for a company growing as fast as it is, in my view. However, the CEO search does introduce some uncertainty. And we still have to account for the risk of margin erosion as industry competition intensifies. So, what's the verdict? Nvidia looks like a buy at current levels, but it's hardly a once-in-a-decade buying opportunity. Still, investors who purchase the company's shares today could see strong returns over the medium term.
